title: Cut priority stack: feeling first, geography last
when: Whenever two candidate shots or two candidate cut points compete and the editor must pick one.
summary: Judge every cut by what it does to the viewer in a fixed order: emotional effect, then story progress, then rhythm, then where the eye lands, and only last screen direction and spatial continuity. With stock and generated material there is no continuous physical space, so rhythm and story dominate.
steps: Score the candidate on emotional fit for the current beat (does it build or release tension as the script intends).
Score story contribution (does the incoming shot add information, a turn, or a contrast).
Score rhythm (does its length differ usefully from the last two shots).
Score eye trace (is the incoming subject near where attention already sits).
Check screen direction and spatial logic last.
Choose the best weighted total; perfect continuity never rescues a cut that fails emotion or story.
do: Weight emotion and story far above continuity in any automated cut-scoring function.
Cut on reveals, musical turns and strong visual contrast rather than on information density.
Let a strong image, line or gesture play out instead of covering it with inserts.
avoid: Picking the technically clean shot that adds nothing new.
Burying an emotional moment under extra coverage.
Optimising purely for facts-per-second.

numbers.priority_order: emotion > story > rhythm > eye trace > 2D screen direction > 3D spatial continuity

checks: Every cut in the edit decision list carries a one-line reason naming its emotional or story job.
Hero-flagged moments contain no inserted cutaway.

title: Average shot length and cuts-per-minute by style
when: When assigning hold durations to a sequence after its style or register is known.
summary: Average shot length is the main energy dial. Pick the band for the style, then vary individual holds around that average in a breathing pattern rather than cutting at a constant interval.
steps: Classify the sequence: action, standard cinematic, documentary, contemplative, or montage.
Take the average-shot-length band and cuts-per-minute range for that class.
Lay holds out as a breathing curve: long, medium, short, short, very long, medium.
Reject any run where three consecutive shots have the same length; re-distribute time.
do: Use short holds for urgency and long holds for weight, grief or awe.
Follow a cluster of quick shots with one long hold so the viewer can breathe.
Let the longest holds fall on the most important images.
avoid: Metronome cutting where every shot is the same length.
Three shots of identical length back to back.
Using montage-speed cutting for documentary narration.
checks: Computed cuts-per-minute of each sequence falls inside its style band.
No three consecutive cut durations are equal (use a small tolerance such as +/-0.25 s).

title: Something must change: micro and macro change cadence
when: Building any timeline longer than about a minute, to keep the screen from going stale.
summary: A viewer absorbs a new image in roughly 3 s and starts drifting after about 5 s without change. Schedule a small visual or audio change every few seconds, a substantive frame change every 20-30 s, and never let 15 s pass with nothing new. In long-form the primary cut interval starts fast in the hook and relaxes, with micro-changes filling gaps.
steps: Mark the phases: hook (0:00-0:30), early body (0:30-3:00), mid body (3:00-7:00), late body (8:00+).
Set the primary cut interval per phase from the numbers below.
Between primary cuts, schedule micro-changes (slow push-in, text pop, overlay, SFX, caption emphasis) so no 5 s window is static.
Ensure each script section carries at least one visual cue per 8-10 s of narration.
do: Treat zoom moves, overlays and sound accents as legitimate changes that reset attention.
Front-load cut density in the first 30 s, then stabilise.
In late body alternate calm stretches with short bursts.
avoid: A single still or clip held more than 15 s with no movement, text or sound event.
Planning one visual per script section when the section runs long.
Static images for narration that describes a process or transformation.

numbers.late_body: 15-25 s calm plus a burst every 2-3 min
numbers.visual_cue_density: at least 1 per 8-10 s of script (60 s video = 6-8 cues)

checks: Longest gap between any visual or audio event is <= 5 s in the hook and <= 15 s anywhere.
Each script section has at least one enhancement or visual cue per 10 s of its duration.
Primary cut intervals per phase fall inside the phase band.

title: Short-form (Shorts/Reels/TikTok) pacing and structure
when: Cutting any vertical video under about 60 s, or a Shorts cut-down of a long video.
summary: Short-form runs two to three times faster than long-form: a visual change every 1-3 s, no static hold over 3 s, fast narration, music from frame one, and a beat structure that ends by looping back to the start. Total watch time, not just completion, is what gets rewarded.
steps: Pick duration from the completion table (15 s single fact, 30 s one concept, 60 s mini-tutorial).
Budget words for that duration.
Use the beat template: hook 0-1 s, context, content with a visual change every 2-3 s, payoff/result, CTA or loop.
Speed-ramp setup material (1.2-1.5x) and return to 1.0x for the payoff.
End on a frame that flows back into the opening so replays feel seamless.
do: Start voice, text and music on frame one.
Use word-by-word captions and 3-5 word on-screen text blocks.
Prefer 21-34 s on TikTok for completion; Shorts performs at roughly 13 s or a full 60 s.
avoid: Any intro, logo, or greeting before the point.
Dead air or long pauses (a pause reads as a reason to scroll).
Holding any static frame longer than 3 s.

numbers.interrupt_effect: interrupts every 2-4 s ~58% avg retention vs ~41% for static talking head

checks: First narration onset and first text both occur within 0.5 s.
No shot or hold exceeds 3 s without a visual change.
Word count within the budget for the chosen duration.
Last frame visually connects to the first (loop check by frame similarity).

title: Building the opening hook (first 3 s and first 30 s)
when: Assembling the first seconds of any video, short or long.
summary: The open must earn every next second: a striking moving image on frame one, text inside half a second, narration immediately, and in long-form a fixed run of visual hook, verbal hook, stakes and an open loop that is complete by 0:30. Pick the hook archetype from the content type.
steps: Choose the archetype: contrarian (myth-busting), outcome promise, mystery (dated, story-led), stakes (cost of a mistake); for short-form also result-first, bold claim text, question, or visual pattern interrupt.
0:00-0:03: the single most compelling moving shot in the video; it must deliver what the thumbnail promised.
0:03-0:08: the verbal hook (question or promise) in one or two sentences.
0:08-0:15: stakes - why the viewer should care.
0:15-0:30: preview the payoff and plant an unanswered question that will be resolved later.
0:30-0:35: optional brand sting, 5 s maximum, never before the hook.
Cut every 3-5 s during this window and narrate at the faster hook pace.
do: Open on motion, a face, or the end result.
Put hook text on screen inside 0.5 s so muted viewers get it.
Create curiosity first; hold facts back for the payoff.
Use a pattern interrupt inside the first 5 s.
avoid: Black frames, logos, title cards or greetings at the start.
Announcing the format ('in this video we will look at...').
Dumping technical facts as the first line.
Revealing the best moment in the opening seconds and leaving nothing to wait for.
A static first frame.

numbers.early_interrupt_gain: +23% average retention when an interrupt lands in the first 5 s

checks: Frame 0 is not black, not a logo card, and differs from frame 12 (motion present).
First narration onset < 0.5 s.
Open-loop tag exists in the script before 0:30 and a matching resolution tag exists later.
Opening frames are visually similar to the thumbnail.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/short-form.md; skills/creative/long-form.md; skills/creative/storytelling.md; skills/pipelines/explainer/script-director.md; skills/pipelines/clip-factory/edit-director.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Retention curve defence for 3-15 minute videos
when: Planning or reviewing any video over about 3 minutes, including 5-7 minute faceless documentaries.
summary: Audience loss clusters at predictable points: the 30-second cliff, a valley around 2-3 minutes when initial curiosity is spent, a second exodus around 55-65% of runtime, and the final 20 s. Place a specific countermeasure at each.
steps: Plant at least one open question in the first 60 s and hold its answer back.
Deliver a first real payoff (a down-payment on the hook's promise) before 2:00.
Put a pattern interrupt at 1:45-2:00 (angle/style shift, burst of quick B-roll, music change).
Insert a spoken re-hook around 2:00 and then every 3-4 minutes (a line that promises the next part is stranger, bigger or the twist).
At 55-65% of runtime resolve an open loop and run a burst sequence.
Keep the last 20 s free of essential content; tease the next video instead of saying goodbye.
do: Write re-hook lines as concrete promises about what comes next.
Use foreshadowing ('the surprising part is a minute away') to bridge calm sections.
Treat any section whose projected retention falls under 30% as needing an interrupt.
avoid: A calm unbroken explanation through 2:00-3:00.
Goodbyes and summaries that signal the video is over.
Critical visuals in the end-screen zone.

numbers.ai_narration_risk: AI voice linked to ~35% extra drop in first 45 s

checks: Script has an open-loop marker before 60 s and its resolution after the midpoint.
A payoff marker exists before 120 s.
Re-hook markers exist near 120 s and at least every 240 s after.
No narration-critical visual sits in the final 20 s.

title: Pattern interrupt schedule and burst sequences
when: Laying out the body of a narrated video so attention is reset on a known schedule.
summary: Mix cheap minor interrupts every 20-30 s with major interrupts every 60-90 s, and every 2-3 minutes fire a burst of 5-10 rapid cuts over 10-15 s before returning to calm. Interrupts should be motivated by content, not random.
steps: Place minor interrupts every 20-30 s: B-roll cutaway, stat or definition text, a direct-address line, an SFX accent, a punch-in.
Place major interrupts every 60-90 s: visual style change, music energy shift, new section treatment.
Every 2-3 minutes build a burst: 5-10 quick cuts in 10-15 s, then settle.
Insert a palette cleanser (short visual breather, light moment, or 'let that land' pause) every 45-60 s.
do: Tie each interrupt to a content event (a number triggers a stat pop, a new topic triggers a style change).
Rotate interrupt types so the pattern itself does not become predictable.
In short-form, interrupt every 2-4 s.
avoid: Interrupting a deliberate silence or emotional hold.
Using the same interrupt (e.g., identical whoosh-zoom) every time.
Long talking stretches beyond 30-60 s without a cutaway.

numbers.palette_cleanser: every 45-60 s, ~5 s long in a 3-min arc

checks: Gap between consecutive interrupts never exceeds 30 s (minor) / 90 s (major).
At least one burst sequence per 3 minutes of body.
No interrupt is placed inside a marked silence window.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/long-form.md; skills/creative/storytelling.md; skills/creative/short-form.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: But/therefore causality and misconception-first structure
when: Writing or reviewing narration for explainers and documentaries.
summary: Join sections with contradiction ('but') or consequence ('therefore'), never with plain addition. Open with what the audience wrongly believes, let the obvious explanation partly work and then fail, reveal one key insight, and follow it with silence. Keep one new idea per 30-45 s.
steps: Setup: state what viewers think they know.
But: show why it is incomplete or wrong.
Therefore: introduce the real mechanism.
But: that mechanism raises a new puzzle.
Therefore: deliver the answer, then show how it changes the original belief.
After the key insight, mark 1-3 s of silence and hold the visual.
Build complex visuals layer by layer, each layer arriving as narration names it.
do: Lead with a misconception for science/history topics (it measurably improves learning and engagement).
Add a spoken signpost every 30-45 s ('here is where it turns').
Remove interesting-but-irrelevant asides.
avoid: 'And then... and then...' chains.
Seductive detail tangents (they cut transfer learning by roughly 20-30%).
Showing the full picture before the narration has built up to it.
Putting new information in the closing lines.

numbers.concept_density: at most one fresh idea every 30-45 s
numbers.offset_penalty: visual offset from narration by a few seconds ~30% learning drop

checks: Flag section transitions that start with 'and then' or similar additive connectors.
Count new concepts per 45 s window; flag > 1.
A silence marker follows the climax/insight section.

title: Arc and chapter timing scaled by runtime
when: Allocating seconds to hook, tension, core, proof and close for a target runtime.
summary: Use a proportional arc: short hook, tension/information gap, a long core of concepts, a concrete proof/example, then implications and a close that calls back to the hook. Longer videos become chapters of 2-4 minutes each, at most 5-6 chapters.
steps: Look up the row for the target length (interpolate for in-between lengths such as 6-7 min).
Assign the concept count; each concept gets one visual idea.
Place the palette cleanser between complication and key insight.
Make the close a callback to the opening hook plus one-sentence restatement.
For 8+ minute videos split into chapters with a mini-hook at each boundary and add timestamps.
do: Make the key insight the most polished visual in the video.
Place a subscribe ask only after value has been delivered (around the middle).
Use the cinematic beat map (hook, escalation, reveal, landing, plus a midpoint turn if long) for non-explainer pieces.
avoid: More than 5-6 chapters in 10-15 minutes (feels fragmented).
More than 1 info card per 2 minutes.
A close that introduces new material.

numbers.1_min: 1-2 concepts; hook 5 s, tension 10 s, core 30 s, proof 10 s, close 5 s
numbers.2_min: 2-3 concepts; hook 8, tension 15, core 60, proof 25, close 12 (s)
numbers.3_min: 3-5 concepts; hook 8, tension 22, core 100, proof 30, close 15 (s)
numbers.5_min: 5-8 concepts; hook 10, tension 30, core 180, proof 50, close 20 (s)

checks: Sum of section durations equals target runtime within +/-5%.
Concept count does not exceed the row maximum.
Closing section references a phrase or image from the hook.

title: Narration word budget and TTS duration feedback loop
when: Before generating TTS, and again after TTS returns real durations.
summary: Narration should fill about 85-90% of runtime so visuals can breathe. Budget words from a speaking rate, then measure the real TTS duration per section and either rewrite or stretch the scene when audio overruns.
steps: Pick a pace: ~150-160 WPM explainer, 140-150 cinematic/insight, 180-200 short-form.
Words allowed = runtime x 0.85-0.90 x words-per-second (2.0-2.5 documentary, 2.5-3.0 energetic).
Split by scene proportional to scene length, leaving 0.5-1 s of silence at scene changes.
Generate TTS, probe each section's actual seconds.
If a section runs > 1.15x its slot: rewrite shorter, or (if no more than ~25% over) extend the visual slot.
If total narration exceeds the video by > 1 s, cut words or extend the closing scene.
do: Vary pace by section: hook faster, explanation steady, key insight slower, conclusion lifts.
Keep opening and closing scenes lightly narrated.
Count words before every TTS call.
avoid: Writing 250 words for 60 s (the audio either rushes or the video balloons).
Cutting visuals to planned durations instead of measured audio durations.

numbers.wpm_by_section: hook 160-170; explanation 150-160; key insight 140-150; silence 1-3 s; conclusion 155-165

checks: Measured TTS seconds per section <= slot seconds (or slot extended and logged).
Total narration <= video duration, and overrun never > 1 s.
Script word count within +/-10% of budget.

title: Directing TTS narration with concrete delivery cues
when: Any time narration will be synthesised (e.g., ElevenLabs).
summary: Generated voice sounds read rather than performed unless it is directed. Write a whole-video performance plan plus per-section cues (pace, energy, emphasis words, pauses, a delivery note, and provider text with explicit break tags), then approve a sample before batch generation.
steps: Write a top-level plan: intent, pacing profile, energy curve across the video, pause policy.
For each section give at least two concrete cues: pace, energy, emphasis words, pause before/after (seconds), delivery note, provider-ready text with breaks.
Put a breath ahead of any twist, right after a startling fact, and ahead of the closing point.
Render a test clip of whichever section is hardest to perform well (rarely the opening one).
Approve or adjust settings, record them, then batch-generate from the structured provider text.
do: Write for the ear: short sentences, light contractions, clear punctuation.
Keep one delivery idea per section; split sections that need several emotional turns.
For ElevenLabs lower stability for variation, moderate style, speed within 0.7-1.2, keep similarity high.
Add pronunciation guides for names, acronyms and foreign terms.
avoid: Directions like 'natural' or 'engaging' without a measurable cue.
Sprinkling so many breaks that the read turns theatrical.
Changing voice, model or speed after sample approval without a new sample.
Generating from raw script text when structured cue text exists.

numbers.typical_pause: 0.2-0.7 s (0.6 s before a question in the example)

checks: Every narrated section has >= 2 delivery cues.
A sample file and its provider settings are recorded before batch TTS.
Final TTS settings equal the approved sample settings.

title: Processing chain for AI narration before the mix
when: After TTS generation and before mixing narration with music and SFX.
summary: TTS voices have uneven dynamics, boxy low-mids and harsh sibilance. Clean them with a fixed chain: high-pass, mud cut, presence lift, sibilance tame, firm compression, de-ess and a true-peak limiter, then confirm intelligibility on a phone-sized speaker.
steps: High-pass at 80-100 Hz (steep, ~24 dB/oct).
Cut around 500 Hz to remove boxiness.
Boost 2-5 kHz by 2-3 dB for presence; gently cut 6-8 kHz.
Optionally add 120-250 Hz body for thin voices.
Compress ~3:1, attack 1-5 ms, release 10-20 ms (30 ms if pumping), threshold ~-26 dB for 4-6 dB gain reduction, ~+6 dB makeup.
De-ess at 6-8 kHz if needed; notch narrow artifacts in 4-6 kHz.
Limit at -1.5 dBTP.
do: Compress AI narration more firmly than you would a human take.
Check on phone speakers; if the voice vanishes, lift 2-4 kHz further.
avoid: Sending raw TTS straight into the mix.
Letting the limiter do the job of the compressor.

numbers.compressor: 3:1 (2:1-4:1), 1-5 ms attack, 10-20 ms release, -26 dB threshold, +6 dB makeup

checks: Narration stem true peak <= -1.5 dBTP.
Short-term loudness of narration varies within a narrow band (no section 3+ LU quieter than others).

title: Music ducking depth and sidechain settings
when: Mixing a music bed under narration.
summary: Music under speech should sit roughly 18-20 dB below the voice, with an EQ notch in the speech band, and be ducked automatically by a sidechain keyed from narration. Err quieter than feels right.
steps: Start the bed about 20 dB under narration and adjust in 1 dB steps.
Cut 2-4 kHz on the music to clear the intelligibility band.
Sidechain-compress music from the narration (threshold ~0.02, ratio ~9, attack ~200 ms, release ~500 ms).
Duck harder (up to ~22 dB) for dense educational passages.
Fade music in (1-2 s) and out (3-4 s) at the ends.
do: Drop an extra ~4 dB below the level that first seems right (broadcast practice).
Keep the bed continuous across a long-form video (no silent gaps unless a deliberate dropout).
Use lower beds in short-form (-22 to -26 dB).
avoid: Full-level music under narration.
Lyrics under narration.
Music cutting abruptly at a clip boundary.

numbers.duck_depth: 6-12 dB typical, up to 22 dB for complex topics
numbers.sidechain: threshold 0.02, ratio 9, attack 200 ms, release 500 ms

checks: Measured music-only loudness during narration is >= 18 dB below narration loudness.
Narration remains intelligible in a phone-speaker simulation.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/sound-design.md; skills/core/ffmpeg.md; skills/creative/long-form.md; skills/creative/video-stitching.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Loudness targets and delivery encode spec
when: Final mix and export for YouTube, Shorts and other platforms.
summary: Deliver at -14 LUFS integrated with true peak under -1.5 dBTP for YouTube, keep chapter-to-chapter loudness steady, and encode H.264 at high quality with web-friendly flags.
steps: Normalise each clip/stem (around -16 LUFS) before assembly.
Mix, then measure integrated loudness, loudness range and true peak.
Apply final limiter and loudness normalisation to the platform target.
Encode H.264 CRF 18-20, yuv420p, faststart; AAC 192 kbps+, 48 kHz.
do: Measure loudness per chapter and keep differences under 2 LU.
Keep 6-12 dB dynamic range for speech-led content.
avoid: Exceeding -1.5 dBTP (YouTube) or -1 dBTP (TikTok/IG).
Short-form bitrates under ~5 Mbps (triggers platform quality downgrade).
checks: Integrated loudness within +/-1 LU of target.
True peak below the platform ceiling.
Per-chapter integrated loudness spread < 2 LU.
Output pixel format yuv420p and moov atom at file start.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/sound-design.md; skills/core/ffmpeg.md; skills/creative/long-form.md; skills/creative/animation-pipeline.md; skills/creative/short-form.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Choosing the music bed: tempo, key, dynamics
when: Selecting or generating music for a video or a section.
summary: Match tempo and key to content and mood, keep it instrumental under narration, choose dynamically even beds for explainers and dynamic swelling scores for cinematic pieces, and stay on one track unless the story genuinely turns.
steps: Map the content type to a BPM band.
Map the mood to a key family.
For explainers choose steady, even tracks; for cinematic/reveal sections choose dynamic tracks with swells and quiet passages.
Ideally get a track as long as the video; otherwise loop a long track with 2-3 s crossfades at loop points.
If using sections (intro, main, reveal, outro), crossfade them over 2-3 s and keep tempo within +/-10 BPM.
do: Shift music energy at chapter boundaries.
Change key or instrumentation at narrative turning points (cinematic).
Include 'background/underscore' intent when generating music.
avoid: Vocals or lyrics under narration.
Beat drops and sudden crescendos under explanation.
Busy bright hi-hats or lead lines in the 2-4 kHz speech band.
Switching music style mid-video without a story reason.

numbers.keys: happy C/G major; serious D/A minor; mysterious E/B minor; triumphant D/Bb major; melancholy F/C minor
numbers.section_map: intro 8-10 s building; main steady; reveal 20-30 s fuller; outro 10-15 s fading

checks: Music duration >= video duration (or loop plan exists).
Track flagged instrumental.
BPM spread across the video <= 20 BPM.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/sound-design.md; skills/creative/music-gen-usage.md; skills/creative/cinematic.md; skills/creative/long-form.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Cutting to the music: downbeats, one held silence, tail fade
when: Locking cut points in montage, documentary and cinematic sequences.
summary: Music is the timing grid you cut to, not garnish added at the end. Land hero cuts on downbeats, drop the music out once at the emotional centre, and let it fade under the final image.
steps: Get beat times from a beat tracker, or compute them from BPM (beat = 60/BPM s).
Snap hero cuts to the nearest downbeat; with no beat data, default to cuts every 4 beats (every 4 s at 60 BPM).
Reorder adjacent slots if that lands a hero image on a strong beat.
Place one silence window (~2 s) right before the emotional peak; for cinematic reveals pull music for 3-5 s.
Ramp the music back after the window with a short (~0.2 s) hold-off.
Fade music under the last 3-5 s so the final image breathes without a musical cadence fighting it.
do: Use silence exactly once per piece and use it decisively.
Leave 1-3 s of quiet after a key insight in explainers.
avoid: Choosing music after the cut is locked.
Multiple dropouts that dilute the effect.
A music ending that resolves before or after the picture ends.
checks: Each hero cut lies within a few frames of a beat.
Music level inside the silence window measures near silence (around -60 dB).
Music fade-out begins 3-5 s before the end.

title: Sound effect placement and timing
when: Adding whooshes, pops, risers and impacts to transitions, text and reveals.
summary: Sound slightly leads picture because the brain processes audio faster: start a whoosh 10-20 ms before the visual change and align its peak with the moment of greatest visual change. Each SFX type has a length and level band below the narration.
steps: Pick the SFX type for the event (transition, text appearance, UI tap, build-up, reveal).
Set its level band and duration from the table.
Offset start 10-20 ms ahead of the visual; align the energy peak with the biggest frame change.
Nudge in single-frame steps until it feels locked.
If stacking whooshes, use different frequency bands.
do: Use a riser to build into a reveal and an impact on the reveal or key statistic.
Use soft pops for bullet/text appearances.
Keep SFX at least 6 dB under the dialogue.
avoid: SFX louder than narration.
Identical whoosh on every cut.
Adding ambience or effects just to fill a gap the plan did not call for.
checks: Every transition SFX onset precedes its visual change by 0-20 ms (or up to 1 frame).
No SFX peak exceeds the narration peak.

title: Four-layer sound: narration, music, ambience, effects
when: Designing the soundtrack of documentary or cinematic sequences.
summary: A professional soundtrack is more than voice plus music: add a low ambient bed that matches the scene (city, nature, lab, room tone) to give presence during pauses, plus selective effects at key moments, each at its own level band.
steps: Narration as the primary layer.
Music bed under it at its ducked level.
Ambient/room-tone bed matching the on-screen environment, very low.
Foley/SFX only at key actions and reveals.
Discard stock-clip audio by default; reintroduce selected ambience deliberately.
do: Keep a subtle ambience running so narration pauses never fall into digital silence.
For intimate moments drop music entirely and keep voice plus room tone.
avoid: Raw stock-clip audio left in the mix.
Mismatched ambience across a cut inside the same scene.

numbers.ambient: -30 to -24 dB (room tone around -35 dB; moody beds ~-28 dB)
numbers.quiet_moments: around -24 LUFS within a -14 LUFS mix

checks: No unintended digital-silence gaps > 1 s in the final mix.
Ambient stem present for scenes flagged as needing presence.

title: J-cuts and L-cuts to weld shots together
when: Joining two shots where a hard simultaneous audio/video cut would feel abrupt.
summary: Offset sound from picture: in a J-cut the next shot's audio starts before its picture (anticipation); in an L-cut the current shot's audio continues under the next picture (lingering). Carrying ambience across a cut binds two images more tightly than any visual transition.
steps: Pick J when the next beat should be heard before it is seen (builds anticipation, introduces a new place by its sound).
Pick L when the feeling of the outgoing shot should linger, or for a smooth exit.
Offset dialogue/narration by 0.3-0.5 s; carry ambient sound 0.5-1.5 s.
Fade the overlapping audio out over the overlap so it does not stack.
Reserve the technique for the 3-4 hardest transitions in a short piece.
do: Carry strong ambience (rain, traffic, footsteps) from the outgoing clip.
Use J-cuts at section starts so the new topic's sound pulls the viewer in.
avoid: Every cut as an L/J cut (it blurs structure).
Overlapping two narration lines.

numbers.claimed_effect: montages with L-cuts feel markedly more coherent

checks: Overlap regions have a fade on the outgoing audio.
L/J offsets fall inside the stated ranges.

title: Transition grammar: when each transition is right or wrong
when: Choosing the join between any two shots or sections.
summary: The hard cut is the default and the most invisible, professional transition. Every other transition carries meaning (time passing, new section, deeper detail, next step), so use a small fixed vocabulary consistently and reserve special transitions for real structural moments.
steps: Same scene / continuous action or same topic with a new angle: hard cut (smooth audio with J/L).
Topic change: crossfade 0.5-1.0 s.
Passing time or a change of mood: crossfade of 1.0-1.5 s.
Major section break (intro to body, body to outro, act break): fade through black 0.5-1.0 s each side.
Motion graphics only: wipe/slide = next step (0.5-0.8 s); zoom in = going deeper, zoom out = bigger picture (0.8-1.2 s); morph = concept evolving (1-2 s); match cut = same shape, new content.
Scale durations to pace: fast short-form 0.3-0.5 s; medium 0.5-1.0 s; slow documentary 1.0-1.5 s crossfades.
do: Lock 2-3 transition types (documentary max 4) for the whole video.
Use fade-in on the first shot and fade-out on the last (0.5-1.0 s).
If a sequence feels boring, fix clip choice or pacing instead of adding transitions.
avoid: Wipes, push/slide, zoom blurs, RGB splits, light leaks and glitch effects in documentary register (they read as social-media editing).
A dissolve on every cut (reads as indecision).
Three different transition types inside the first 15 s.
Random transition variety with no meaning.
checks: Distinct transition types in the EDL <= 4.
Hard cuts are the majority of joins.
No banned transition types in documentary/cinematic presets.
First 15 s uses at most 2 transition types.

title: Hold-length table by emotional register
when: Converting a tone (elegiac, urgent, etc.) and a duration into hold lengths and shot counts.
summary: Each emotional register has a base, minimum and maximum hold. Hero shots get the maximum, ordinary cutaways the base, quick connective shots the minimum; the total must land within 10% of the target and non-hero holds are compressed first.
steps: Pick one register for the piece or section.
Number of shots ~ duration / base hold (or use the slots-per-60 s figure).
Assign max hold to hero shots (opening, turn, final), base to cutaways, min to quick connectors.
Sum holds; if off by more than +/-10%, adjust non-hero holds first, never shorten heroes to fit.
Choose a shape: list (uniform accumulation), before/after (half, pivot, half), three-act (30/40/30), or one image explored from many angles.
do: Use this for B-roll rhythm inside narrated sections as well as pure montage.
Re-check that cut count matches duration (too many cuts = nausea, too few = slideshow).
avoid: 45 s with ~50 cuts (unless intentionally urgent).
3 minutes with only ~12 cuts.
Mixing registers within one short piece without a turn.

numbers.elegiac: base 4.0 s, min 2.5, max 7.0; ~15 shots per 60 s
numbers.reverent: base 3.5 s, min 2.0, max 6.0; ~17 per 60 s
numbers.dreamlike: base 3.0 s, min 1.5, max 5.5; ~20 per 60 s
numbers.wry: base 2.0 s, min 1.0, max 4.0; ~30 per 60 s
numbers.urgent: base 1.2 s, min 0.5, max 2.5; ~50 per 60 s

checks: Sum of holds within +/-10% of target.
Hero cuts have the longest holds in their neighbourhood.
Every hold within its register's min-max range.

title: Trim each clip to its single best moment
when: Setting in/out points on stock or generated clips.
summary: A long stock clip usually holds one short moment worth showing surrounded by setup and settle. Find that sub-window, leave the shot just before its action finishes (on a look, not a walk-off), keep a few frames of handle, and never fake length with a freeze.
steps: Scan the clip for its peak (motion energy, subject facing camera, the action itself).
Centre the hold on that peak; cut out before the action naturally completes.
Leave 4-6 frames of handle at both ends for fades.
If the clip is shorter than the hold: slow it to 0.5-0.75x only if it is near-static with no faces or lip movement; otherwise borrow time from the neighbour slot or swap to the second-ranked clip.
do: End shots on a gaze or a held pose so the cut feels chosen.
Keep a rejected-picks list so a replacement is one step away.
avoid: Using the first N seconds of a clip by default.
Letting a shot run until its action is exhausted.
Freeze-framing the last frame to fill time (reads as an error).
Slow-motion on talking faces or synced motion.

numbers.typical_ratio: ~3 s usable moment inside a ~12 s stock clip

checks: No frozen run longer than a few frames in the output (freeze detection).
Speed < 1.0 used only on clips with low motion and no detected faces.
Out point >= handle frames before the source clip end.

title: Adjacent-shot diversity rules
when: After shots are chosen and ordered, before render.
summary: Most slideshow feel comes from neighbours that look alike. Walk the timeline in pairs and break any repetition of subject+scale, palette, motion direction, scene type or shot size; give hero shots a scale different from their neighbours.
steps: For each consecutive pair, compare subject and shot scale; if both match, swap one for a different scale (wide vs close).
Track dominant colour; break runs of the same palette at least every 4 cuts.
Compare motion direction; if two pans go the same way, flip or reorder.
Check scene-type runs and shot-size runs across the whole plan.
Make sure no clip is used in two slots.
do: Alternate wide establishing and close detail shots for rhythm.
Log every swap with its reason.
avoid: Two near-identical clips back to back.
Same Ken Burns direction or pan direction repeatedly.
The same clip winning several slots.

numbers.shot_size_dominance_limit: > 50% of scenes with one size is a violation
numbers.same_size_run_limit: 3 consecutive same-size shots is a violation

checks: No adjacent pair shares subject AND scale (embedding or tag similarity).
No adjacent near-duplicate frames (perceptual hash distance above threshold).
Longest run of same scene type <= 3; distinct types >= 3.
Hero shot size differs from both neighbours.
Each source clip id appears once.

title: Matching B-roll to narration: literal vs metaphorical
when: Deciding what to show under each narration sentence.
summary: Concrete references (places, objects, people, events, equipment, history) get literal real footage; abstract mechanisms and ideas get diagrams, generated metaphors or analogy visuals. If it must look real, source it; if it must look specific to this concept, generate or draw it. Meaning can also come from juxtaposing two ordinary shots.
steps: For each sentence ask: what is being talked about, is it concrete or abstract, is there an embedded visual cue, and how long is it.
Concrete: literal stock/archive footage matching the noun.
Abstract process: diagram or animated build; abstract quality (growth, connection): metaphorical image or generated clip.
Write a brief per need: time range, description, source type, 2-4 keywords, duration, orientation, mood, fallback.
Where a single image cannot say it, pair two shots so their contrast states the idea.
do: Prefer real stock for people and real places (generated people often look uncanny).
Use archive sources for historical claims.
Trust a plain image: if the footage already shows it, do not also explain it with text.
Aim for B-roll to cover roughly 35-50% of an educational video if a presenter exists; faceless videos are effectively all B-roll, so vary its kind.
avoid: Keyword-matched but irrelevant footage.
Pretty but unrelated 'seductive' visuals.
Generic metaphors (handshake, lightbulb) for every abstract idea.
Mixing real footage and fantasy/AI style in children's content.
checks: Every narration sentence maps to a visual with a stated literal/metaphor/diagram type.
Concrete-noun sentences use literal footage unless a reason is logged.

title: Visual lands on the spoken word (temporal contiguity)
when: Timing cuts, overlays and reveals against narration.
summary: What the narrator names must be on screen as it is said; learning and engagement fall sharply when picture and voice drift apart. Use word timestamps from the narration to anchor cuts and overlays, and reveal complex visuals piece by piece in step with the words.
steps: Transcribe the final narration to word-level timestamps.
Tag keywords that trigger visuals (nouns, numbers, names, 'look at...').
Snap the matching cut or overlay to the keyword onset (or the start of its sentence).
For diagrams and lists, add each element as it is spoken.
Verify every scene's narration ends before its visual does.
do: Prefer cutting at sentence or phrase boundaries rather than mid-word.
Hold a visual a beat past its line rather than cutting before the line ends.
avoid: Planned durations instead of measured narration timing.
Showing the whole diagram before narration reaches it.
Narration about X over a visual of Y.

numbers.underfill_fail: visual frozen > 5 s after its last step
numbers.learning_penalty: ~30% drop when offset by a few seconds

checks: For every cut, |narration segment start - visual start| <= 0.5 s.
Keyword-triggered overlays appear within +/-0.5 s of the word.
No scene where narration continues past its visual's end.

title: Writing stock-footage search queries
when: Turning a shot need into searches on Pexels, Pixabay and archive libraries.
summary: Stock search is keyword matching, not understanding. Use 2-4 words that lead with the subject, add a point-of-view term (drone, macro, top-down...), write two or three differently-angled queries per shot, and reword rather than repeat when results are weak.
steps: Literal query: the phrase a stock user would type (subject + action).
Lateral query: same idea from another scale or angle.
Association query (for hero shots): an adjacent concept that may surface texture shots.
Append a POV/technique word: aerial, drone, close-up, macro, top-down, handheld, locked-off, timelapse, slow motion, over-the-shoulder, dashcam.
Filter by orientation, min/max duration and min width.
On failure try synonyms, then another provider, then generation, then ask the user.
do: Use period vocabulary for vintage briefs ('commuter', 'housewife', 'suburb').
Use templates: place+time+POV; person+action+POV; object+style+POV; element+quality+POV.
Set a minimum duration so you never download clips shorter than the hold.
avoid: Long descriptive sentences or adjective soup as queries.
Category words like 'home' or 'family' that match everything.
Re-running an identical query (results are deterministic).
checks: Every query has <= 5 words and starts with a noun.
Every slot has >= 2 queries; hero slots have 3.

title: Scoring and rejecting candidate footage
when: Choosing one clip per slot from search results.
summary: Score candidates on relevance, style fit, composition, point-of-view, duration and motion, then judge the top few against era, register and neighbouring shots. A similarity score is evidence, not the decision; below a floor, grow the search instead of settling.
steps: Rate each candidate 1-5 (5 use as is; 4 small crop/trim; 3 usable with grade; 2 retry keywords; 1 wrong).
Discard anything under 3 or under the similarity floor.
Among the top 3-5, prefer the one that fits era, emotional register, available hold length and differs from adjacent picks.
If nothing passes, run up to two extra search passes with rewritten queries; then drop or change the slot.
Log each rejected high-scoring clip with its reason.
do: Reject wrong point-of-view shots and re-query instead of cropping (POV errors cost more than grade errors).
Require source duration >= the planned hold.
Build a candidate pool around 8-12x the number of slots.
avoid: Taking the top score blindly (a bright neon city shot can outscore the right sombre one).
Watermarked, shaky (unless intended) or awkwardly cropped subjects.
Static-only pools (they produce slideshows).

numbers.pool_size: 8-12x slot count; < 50 rows is too small

checks: Each slot has exactly one pick with score >= threshold or a logged override.
No clip picked for two slots.
Picked clip duration >= planned hold.
Rejected-picks log exists.

title: Describe shots as images, not feelings
when: Writing shot descriptions, slot lists, scene beats or generation prompts.
summary: Mood words do not constrain pixels. Describe each needed shot the way a location scout would: subject, action or pose, environment, light, era/texture. Translate any mood ('epic', 'moody') into the concrete lighting, grade, framing, hold and audio choices that create it.
steps: Write one thematic question for the piece and keep every slot on it.
Break the theme into sensory, photographable beats.
Use the pattern: who/what; what it is doing; where; what light; period or texture cue.
Mark 2-3 hero slots: opening image, turn, final image.
Replace mood adjectives with recipes (see numbers).
When focus moves between subjects, name it: reveal, disappear, switch, or alternate, and say whether camera or subject causes it.
do: Be specific enough to recognise, loose enough to be surprised by a better shot.
Give hero slots more queries and bigger candidate pools.
Re-read the theme after drafting to catch drift.
avoid: Emotion words or intentions ('a moment of hesitation') as descriptions.
Generic words: beautiful, stunning, modern, futuristic, cutting-edge, innovative, seamless, dynamic, vibrant, amazing.
The word 'cinematic' as an instruction.

numbers.epic: 2.39:1 letterbox, 24 fps, 8 s+ holds, orchestral build
numbers.moody: dark grade ~0.6, low fill light, 6 s+ holds, ambient bed ~-28 dB
numbers.intimate: 1.85:1, 40-50 mm look, shallow focus, voice + room tone only
numbers.music_swell_recipe: state dropout time, silence length (e.g., 1.5 s) and the returning instrument
numbers.generic_language_limit: >= 30% of scenes with generic words = revise

checks: Descriptions contain no words from the emotion/generic blacklist.
At least two slots flagged hero.
Every slot description names a subject and a lighting/time cue.
source: OpenMontage skills/pipelines/documentary-montage/scene-director.md; skills/creative/storytelling.md; skills/creative/cinematic.md; lib/variation_checker.py (heuristics) (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Chaining AI video clips without visible seams
when: Joining several short AI-generated clips into one continuous sequence.
summary: AI clips are short and drift in colour, fps, identity and motion direction. Plan overlap in the prompts, inspect last/first frames at each join, choose a hard cut, short crossfade or fade-through-black by how bad the break is, then unify with one grade and one external soundtrack.
steps: Write prompts so clip N's ending state matches clip N+1's opening state.
Repeat 3-6 identity attributes word-for-word in every prompt (no pronouns like 'the same man').
Conform all clips to one fps and resolution before joining.
Extract the last frame of N and first frame of N+1; compare colour, subject position, background and motion direction.
Good continuity: hard cut or 0.3-0.5 s crossfade; minor break: 0.5-1.0 s crossfade; major break: fade through black (0.5 s out + 0.5 s in).
Apply one global grade after stitching.
Strip generated audio; lay one narration and music track over the whole chain.
do: Prefer fewer, longer clips (e.g., 6 x 10 s rather than 12 x 5 s for 60 s) to halve seams and cost.
Re-roll clips with artifacts using a new seed (a large share of fast-model outputs have them).
Lock a seed once a composition works.
avoid: Motion reversing direction across a join.
Several scene changes requested inside one clip.
Readable text or logos inside generated clips.
Long dialogue lines on fast-cut lip-synced shots (keep to ~6 words).
checks: Boundary-frame difference (histogram or SSIM) above threshold forces crossfade or FTB.
All clips share fps/resolution before concat.
No generated audio tracks remain in the final mix.

title: Technical conformance at every stitch point
when: Concatenating clips or segments into one file.
summary: Most visible amateur errors at joins are technical: mixed fps or codecs, variable frame rate, stretched aspect ratios, clicks at audio cuts, drifting sync and music chopped at a boundary. Conform first, then join, then scrub every seam.
steps: Probe every clip (codec, size, fps, VFR, audio).
Convert VFR to constant frame rate; conform resolution, fps and pixel format.
Fix aspect by padding or cropping; never stretch.
Stream-copy only if everything matches; otherwise re-encode (CRF ~18) the minority clips or all.
At hard audio cuts use a ~5 ms micro-fade or cut at zero crossings.
During crossfades dip the outgoing audio ~6 dB.
Mix music as one continuous track after the video is joined; crossfade music changes 1-2 s centred on the cut.
If one side is silent, fade 0.3 s into/out of the silence.
Compute expected duration as sum of clips minus transition overlaps.
do: Normalise clip loudness before joining.
For 10+ short clips, re-encode to CFR and align the separate audio to the final length to avoid drift.
For picture-in-picture: 20-25% width for commentary, 30-35% for equal importance, bottom-right with ~20 px padding and a 2 px border.
avoid: Concat with stream copy across mismatched GOP or codec settings.
Upscaling or stretching to hide aspect mismatches.
Music that stops dead at a cut.
checks: All inputs share resolution, fps, aspect and codec (or were conformed).
No clicks: no sample discontinuity spikes at cut times.
Output duration equals expected sum within one frame per join.
A/V offset at the end of the file equals offset at the start.

title: Making mixed-source footage look like one film
when: A timeline mixes modern HD stock, archive film, low-res agency footage and AI clips.
summary: Unfinished mixed sources look like a list of internet links. Put everything on one canvas, one aspect treatment, one frame rate and one colour look applied to the whole timeline, and respect low-resolution material instead of blowing it up.
steps: Choose the canvas from the platform (1920x1080 or 1080x1920).
Scale/crop every clip to it; centre-crop 16:9 for vertical.
For low-res or 4:3 archive, letterbox/pillarbox or embrace the boxed look rather than upscaling.
Optionally apply cinematic bars uniformly (~140 px top and bottom at 1080p for ~2.35:1).
Deliver documentary at 24 fps by dropping frames evenly; never blend or interpolate.
Apply one LUT/grade at timeline level; use a lighter strength on already-stylised generated images.
do: Choose the grade by register (warm film for elegiac/dreamlike, cool archive for urgent/wry, near-neutral for reverent, bleach-bypass for harsh).
Log any clip that could not be conformed.
avoid: Per-clip grading (slower and less consistent).
Motion interpolation on mixed footage.
Upscaling 640x480 to full HD.
checks: Every cut renders at the canvas size with no stretching (aspect of active picture preserved).
Exactly one grade/LUT applied across the timeline.
Output fps constant and equal to target.

title: Colour grading decisions and safe parameter ranges
when: Choosing and applying a colour look with FFmpeg filters or a LUT.
summary: Pick a profile by content type rather than defaulting to warm, start at moderate strength, correct before you stylise, apply the creative LUT last, protect skin and keep shadows and highlights off the hard limits.
steps: Choose profile: corporate -> bright/clean; science -> neutral; narrative -> warm; tech/dark UI -> cool; drama -> moody; social -> high contrast; nostalgia -> vintage.
Order: auto-levels if flat, white balance, shadow/mid/highlight balance, curves, contrast/saturation, creative LUT.
Start at about 0.8 strength; change parameters in small steps (~0.05) and review.
Test on one representative frame before the full render.
Check a skin frame and an on-screen-text frame after grading.
do: Lift shadows slightly and roll off highlights (no pure black, no pure white).
Keep saturation <= 1.2 when people are on screen.
Use one profile for the whole video.
avoid: LUTs at 100% strength.
Switching LUTs between scenes.
Orange, green, magenta or grey skin.
Grading that breaks text contrast below 4.5:1.

numbers.profile_strengths: bright_clean 0.8; neutral 1.0; warm 0.85; cool/teal-orange 0.7; moody 0.6-0.7; high contrast 0.8; vintage 0.7
numbers.warm_recipe_magnitude: small red lift/blue cut in shadows and highlights, contrast ~1.05, saturation ~1.08

checks: Text overlay contrast >= 4.5:1 on a graded frame.
Clipped-pixel percentage at 0 and 255 stays near zero.
Same grade parameters used on every clip.
source: OpenMontage skills/core/color-grading.md; skills/creative/cinematic.md; skills/creative/enhancement-strategy.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Cinematic treatment as concrete choices
when: A channel style or video asks for a 'cinematic' look.
summary: Cinematic is a bundle of decisions, not black bars: aspect ratio, 24 fps, longer varied holds, a few designed hero frames, restrained transitions, dynamic music with deliberate silences, layered sound, slower narration and one consistent grade.
steps: Decide aspect: 2.39:1 or 2.35:1 letterbox for true cinematic, 1.85:1 for subtle, plain 16:9 otherwise.
Render pure generated/animated content at 24 fps.
Hold shots 4-8 s on average with deliberate variation.
Designate hero frames: opening image, reveal, final image.
Limit transitions to hard cut, fade to black, slow dissolve and a restrained push-in.
Narrate slower (140-150 WPM); score at 60-90 BPM with dynamics; remove music 3-5 s at the key reveal.
Grade once (warm 0.85 or teal-orange 0.7).
do: Protect quiet moments and impacts in the mix rather than flattening it.
Use title cards sparingly, short and precisely timed.
avoid: Letterboxing screen recordings, talking heads, or footage that needs every pixel.
Default speed ramps and flashy transitions.
Title cards as filler.
Sharpening or grading that damages faces or text.
checks: Hero frames are flagged and fully specified.
If labelled cinematic: >= 1 hero moment, >= 30% of shots with intentional movement, >= 30% with defined lighting.

title: Giving still images purposeful motion (Ken Burns, punch-ins, parallax)
when: A scene is built from photos, generated stills or archive images.
summary: Pan-and-zoom on every still across a whole video reads as a slideshow. Give each still a camera move chosen for meaning (in = closer look, out = context), vary moves between scenes, use 2-3 stills crossfaded per scene, add parallax or light overlays where possible, and keep a healthy share of genuine motion clips.
steps: Choose a move per still: slow zoom in (focus/emphasis), zoom out (reveal context), pan left/right (scan a scene), drift up/down, parallax (layered depth), or static (only with a reason).
Do not repeat the same move/direction on consecutive stills.
Use 2-3 related stills per scene with crossfades for sustained beats.
Use a fast 1.0->1.02 scale bump to mask jump cuts in continuous material.
For detail callouts zoom 1.5-2x with ~0.8 s ease-in-out, hold at least 3 s, return in ~0.6 s.
Track the share of real-motion cuts versus animated stills.
do: Write a reason (shot intent) for every camera move.
Ease every move; never linear position motion.
Mix stills with real stock video and animated graphics.
avoid: Identical Ken Burns on every image.
Movement with no narrative reason.
Promising motion-led video and delivering mostly stills.

numbers.detail_zoom: 1.5-2.0x (UI up to 2.5x), ~0.8 s ease; return ~0.6 s
numbers.static_share_limit: > 60% static/unspecified moves is a violation (aim >= 40% moving)

checks: No two consecutive stills share move type and direction.
Share of static shots <= 60%.
Motion ratio meets the channel's promise.

title: Motion-graphics easing, staging and holds
when: Animating text, graphics, overlays or camera moves on stills.
summary: Nothing should move linearly. Entrances decelerate, exits accelerate, in-scene moves ease both ways; important moves get a tiny anticipation and overshoot; only one thing moves at a time with small staggers; every completed move is followed by a hold long enough to read.
steps: Entrances: ease-out cubic; snappier kinetic type: ease-out quart; playful pops: ease-out back.
Exits: ease-in cubic.
Position/scale/opacity changes inside a scene: ease-in-out cubic or quad.
Add 2-3 frames of anticipation and 10-15% overshoot settling in 3-5 frames on key moves.
Stagger grouped elements 3-6 frames apart, all from the same direction.
Hold after each move per the hold table.
do: Keep linear timing only for opacity or colour.
Use left-to-right motion for progress and right-to-left for going back.
Limit palette to 5 colours with one sparing accent; keep 10% margins.
avoid: Linear motion (robotic).
Everything entering at once.
Gratuitous bounce and spin on serious content.
checks: No keyframed position/scale curve uses linear interpolation.
Multi-element entrances have non-zero stagger.

title: On-screen text: fonts, sizes, safe area, contrast
when: Placing titles, stats, labels, lower thirds or hook text.
summary: Use at most two font families (bold display + neutral body), keep every text element at or above readable minimums, keep text inside title-safe, guarantee contrast with a box, stroke or darkened region, and render exact text as overlays rather than inside AI images.
steps: Pick a pairing (e.g., condensed bold display + clean sans body).
Size titles 60-90 px and body 40-60 px at 1080p; never below 40 px.
Keep text within title-safe (80% of frame).
Add contrast treatment: 70-80% black box, 2-4 px dark stroke, gradient behind text, or 30-50% full-frame dim for text-heavy screens.
Animate in with a 0.3-0.5 s fade or 0.5-1.0 s slide/scale; short-form pops 0.2-0.3 s.
Short-form non-caption text: 3-5 words, upper 40% of the safe zone.
do: Make titles at least 50% larger than body text.
Use sans-serif for anything that moves; serif only for editorial title cards.
Keep overlay lines <= 30 characters and <= 3 lines.
avoid: Script/decorative fonts in body or motion.
Relying on drop shadow alone over busy footage.
Text inside generated images (spellings get hallucinated).
More than two font families.

numbers.lower_third: name 48-60 px bold; role 36-44 px; region 1920x360
numbers.title_safe: 80% (192 px H / 108 px V margins; inner 1536x864)

checks: All text bounding boxes inside title-safe.
Measured contrast of text vs local background >= 4.5:1.
No text element rendered below 40 px at 1080p.
source: OpenMontage skills/creative/typography.md; skills/creative/short-form.md; skills/creative/image-gen-usage.md; skills/pipelines/explainer/scene-director.md (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: How long text must stay on screen
when: Setting the duration of any overlay, title, stat card, chart or end tag.
summary: Hold time is driven by character count and reading speed, plus entrance and exit animation. After the text has fully landed, keep it still for at least characters/13 seconds; title cards sit 3-6 s.
steps: Count characters in the text.
Still-hold = max(floor, characters / 13) seconds after the entrance finishes.
Total = entrance + still-hold + exit.
Clamp to the element's band (title card 3-6 s, overlay 2-5 s, short-form text 2-4 s).
If narration moves on before the hold ends, extend the scene or shorten the text.
do: Use slower reading rates for educational audiences.
Keep charts fully built and still for at least 3 s before cutting away.
avoid: Cutting away from text before it can be read.
Text so long it needs more than ~6 s.

numbers.lower_third: in 1-2 s, display 3-6 s, out 0.5-1 s

checks: For every text element: still-hold >= characters/13 s.
No text element shorter than its band minimum.

title: Caption/subtitle specification for burn-in
when: Generating and burning captions from narration word timestamps.
summary: Captions are mandatory (most mobile viewers watch muted). Group words by cue limits that differ for horizontal and vertical, time cue starts to word onsets with a short tail, style with white text plus outline or a translucent box, and keep them in the bottom band away from key visuals.
steps: Get word-level timestamps for the final narration.
Group words: horizontal 6-8 words/cue and <= 42 chars/line; vertical 3-4 words/cue and ~20-30 chars/line; max 2 lines.
Start each cue at its first word's onset; end ~200 ms after its last word; never run into the next speaker.
Enforce min/max durations and a 2-frame gap between cues.
Style: bold sans, white, black outline (2 px horizontal, 3 px vertical) plus small shadow, or a ~75% black box.
Place in the bottom 20% (horizontal margin ~40, vertical ~50 in ASS units), within 90% of frame width.
For short-form, highlight the active word (karaoke-style).
do: Use the full 8-digit ASS colour form (alpha + BGR), e.g., white = &H00FFFFFF.
Keep sync within 3 frames of audio.
Check every spoken word appears exactly once.
avoid: Oversized vertical captions that fill the centre of the frame.
5+ word cues on vertical (multi-line blocks).
Bottom margins so large that text leaves the frame.
Overlapping cues.

numbers.min_duration: 1 s (0.5 s floor for single-word cues)

checks: No cue exceeds char/word limits for its format.
Cue times monotonic, non-overlapping, gap >= 2 frames.
Caption word sequence equals narration transcript.
Caption box does not overlap other text layers or the safe-zone dead areas.

title: Text layer discipline: no duplicates, no pile-ups
when: Several text layers (captions, hook text, labels, stat cards, watermark, CTA) could appear together.
summary: Decide whether captions carry meaning or are accessibility subtitles, never echo an on-screen headline that narration is already reading, add support layers in a fixed priority order, and scale overlay density to video length. Spoken words plus pictures beat written words plus pictures.
steps: Lock the anchor visual edit first; it must work without overlays.
Add layers in order: subtitles, context labels, diagrams/stat cards, optional inserts, CTA.
At each timestamp count visible text blocks; simplify if they collide.
Remove captions or on-screen text where both say the same line at the same time.
Space overlays by format: short 3-5 s apart, medium 10-20 s, long 30-60 s.
do: Keep overlay positions consistent once chosen.
Let narration carry explanation; use on-screen text for numbers, names, key terms.
avoid: Hook text + subtitles + watermark + lower third all at once.
Title cards and narration explaining the same thing twice.
Decorative overlays with no information.
A video where most scenes are text cards.

numbers.max_text_blocks_at_once: keep to captions + one other block

checks: No timestamp with more than two simultaneous text blocks (captions + one).
Caption text vs on-screen text similarity at the same time below threshold.
Text-card share of scenes <= 40%.

title: Platform safe zones and end-screen zone
when: Placing any text, faces, logos or key visuals for a specific platform.
summary: Platform UI covers parts of the frame: vertical apps hide the bottom ~300 px and a right strip; YouTube end-screen elements cover the last 20 s. Keep important content in the universal vertical safe box and outside end-screen time.
steps: Look up the platform's safe rectangle (vertical) or use title-safe (horizontal).
For multi-platform vertical exports use the universal 900x1400 centred box.
Reserve the final 20 s of long-form for end-screen elements (1-2) and a verbal CTA.
Keep picture-in-picture and badges off captions and key visuals.
do: Preview at real phone size before export.
avoid: Captions or hook text in the bottom 300-320 px of vertical video.
Essential content in the last 20 s of long-form.

numbers.instagram_reels: safe 996x1400; dead top 210, bottom 310, right 84 px
numbers.youtube_shorts: safe 984x1500; dead top 120, bottom 300, right 96 px
numbers.facebook_reels: safe 1080x1520; dead top 100, bottom 300, right 60 px

No new information introduced in the last 20 s of long-form.

title: Charts, stat cards and diagrams in video
when: A beat presents numbers, comparisons, trends or a process.
summary: Video viewers cannot pause or zoom, so data must be simple, animated in step with narration and then held still long enough to read. Choose the form from the data story, cap data points and nodes, build progressively, highlight the point being spoken and keep charts honest.
steps: Fewer than 3 data points or one key number: full-screen stat card, not a chart.

Comparison -> bar (horizontal if labels are long); trend -> line; part-of-whole -> donut (<= 6 slices); KPIs -> 3-6 cards; ranking -> sorted horizontal bars; before/after -> paired bars or delta card.
Build: frame first, data starts ~0.3 s, fully built by 2-4 s, then hold 3-5 s.
Narrated walkthrough: dim non-focus elements to ~30% and highlight the spoken one.
Diagrams: flowchart top-down by default (left-right for timelines), render in stages and crossfade between stages, highlight the current step and dim completed/future ones.
Render diagrams at 4K and downscale for crisp text.
do: Round aggressively ($1,234,567 -> $1.2M) and always show units.
Cite the source in small text.
Use colourblind-safe pairs (blue/orange) and labels, not colour alone.
avoid: Bar axes not starting at zero, 3D charts, dual y-axes, cherry-picked ranges.
Animations under ~1.5-2 s (unreadable) or no hold after.
All elements appearing at once; bouncing/spinning gimmicks.
More than 4-5 colours in one chart.

numbers.highlight: 0.3-0.5 s transition, 2-3 s hold, focus scale ~1.05
numbers.font_minimums_1080p: title 32 px (36-40), axis/value 24 px (28), annotation 20 px, source 16 px
numbers.diagram_text: 3-5 words per node; edge labels 1-2 words

checks: Data point / node counts within limits.
Chart fully built and static for >= 3 s before the cut.
Bar charts start at zero; units and source present.
Any frame during the hold is readable at phone size.

title: Slideshow risk score (automated plan/edit lint)
when: After the scene plan and again after the edit, before spending render time.
summary: Score a plan 0-5 (lower is better) on six dimensions that predict a slideshow feel: repetition, decorative visuals, purposeless motion, missing shot intent, text-card overreliance, and unsupported cinematic claims. Average them into a verdict; also run a variation lint that adds a penalty per violation.
steps: Repetition: +2 if one scene type exceeds 70% of scenes; +1.5 if fewer than 60% of descriptions are unique; +1.5 if one shot size exceeds 60%.
Decorative: share of scenes with no stated information role, narrative role or shot intent, times 5.
Weak motion: among moving shots, share lacking intent, times 4 (no movement at all scores a moderate 1.5).
Weak intent: (1 - share of scenes with shot intent) times 5.
Typography: text/stat-card share > 60% -> 4; > 40% -> 2.5; > 20% -> 1; else 0.
Cinematic claims (only if labelled cinematic): 1.8 per missing element (no hero moment; < 30% shots moving; < 30% with lighting defined).
Average the six; verdict: < 2 strong, < 3 acceptable, < 4 revise, >= 4 fail.

Variation lint: one size > 50% of scenes; a run of 3 same-size shots; > 60% static; <= 1 lighting setup; no hero; hero same size as a neighbour; >= 30% generic wording; < 30% with texture words; < 50% with shot intent. Each violation adds 0.6 (cap 5).
do: Require every scene to carry a one-line purpose (why this frame exists).
Fail the plan before render when the average reaches 4.
avoid: Treating a good verdict as a substitute for watching the render.
Fixing a high score with transitions or effects instead of new shot choices.
checks: Risk average < 3.0 before render.
Score after edit is not higher than score after scene plan.

title: Every cut needs a reason; the ending carries extra weight
when: Final pass on the timeline and when building the last 10-20 s.
summary: If you cannot write one line on why a shot is there, it is arbitrary and should go. The last 5-10 s are remembered out of proportion, so put the strongest image there, fade out cleanly, and optionally land a short thesis line over the final footage instead of a goodbye.
steps: Write a one-line reason for every cut; delete or replace cuts without one.
Check that the final image is among the strongest in the piece; move a stronger candidate to the end if not.
Fade in the first shot (0.5-1.0 s) and fade out the last (0.5-1.5 s), with music fading under the last 3-5 s.
Optional thesis tag: 3-9 words, 5-8 s total (about 1 s in, 3 s hold, 1.5 s out), timed so its fade-out coincides with the picture's fade-out (start = body length - tag length).
Long-form: tease the next video and leave the last 20 s for end-screen elements.
do: Make the tag a thesis, not a summary.
Keep the landing about one feeling or one action.
avoid: 'I need to show this' as a reason for a shot that cannot hold attention.
Freeze-frame endings.
Saying goodbye or recapping everything.
A weak or busy final frame under end text.
checks: Every cut has a non-empty reason string.
Last frame fades to black (mean luma near 0 at the end).
End tag (if any) fade-out aligns with picture fade-out within a few frames.

title: Post-render quality control routine
when: Immediately after every render, before anyone is shown the video.
summary: A render that 'succeeded' can still be silent, cut off, black, stretched or out of sync. Validate inputs before rendering, then probe the file, sample frames at every cut, re-transcribe the audio and compare to the script, measure image quality and loudness, and route each defect back to the stage that can fix it.
steps: Pre-render: all asset paths exist; narration not longer than video; music at least as long as video.
Probe: video and audio streams present (missing audio = stop), resolution matches, duration within +/-5% of target, non-trivial file size.
Sample a frame at the midpoint of every cut (>= 4 frames total) and at first/last frame.
Transcribe the rendered audio: zero words = fail; < 80% of script words = truncated; confirm last scripted words are present.
Image metrics per sampled frame: sharpness, brightness, contrast.
Audio: integrated loudness, true peak, no unintended silences > 1 s, silence window verified if planned.
Visual review: background colours as intended, no blank/stretched images, captions visible and spaced, CTA text exact.
Write each finding with timestamp + concrete fix; route audio issues to mix, visual to sourcing/scene, duration to script, sync to edit.
Allow 2-3 revision rounds, then pass with recorded warnings.
do: Run the checks automatically on every render.
Report findings as accurate (points at a time/field), complete (scan for the same class elsewhere) and constructive (proposes a fix).
avoid: Presenting a render without opening it.
Vague findings like 'pacing feels off'.
Changing edit decisions inside the render step instead of going back to the edit.
checks: ffprobe shows exactly one video and one audio stream with expected codec/size/fps.
Rendered transcript word count >= 0.8 x script word count.
All sampled frames pass blur/brightness/contrast bands.
Integrated loudness and true peak within platform targets.

title: Dead air, fillers and speed ramps
when: Cleaning recorded or synthesised narration and any source with speech pauses.
summary: Trim silences longer than about 1.5 s down to about half a second, keep natural breath and emphasis pauses, cut only at word boundaries, and compress uninteresting process footage with speed ramps while key moments stay at real speed.
steps: Detect silences (around -35 dB, >= 0.5 s) with ~80 ms padding so words are not clipped.
Shorten pauses > 1.5 s to ~0.5 s; keep 0.3-0.8 s breath pauses and intentional dramatic pauses.
Remove fillers and false starts at word boundaries (keep the last clean take).
Choose hard removal (jump cuts) for short-form, or fast-forwarding through silences for long-form.
Speed-ramp process footage: boilerplate 2-3x, navigation 1.5-2x, waiting/building 2-4x or cut, key moments 1.0x.
do: Keep verbal bridges like 'So...' or 'Now...' that carry flow.
Reapply planned pause lengths when stitching TTS sections together.
avoid: Cutting mid-word or clipping word tails.
Removing every pause (breathless, robotic delivery).
Audio pops at cut points.
checks: No unintended silence > 1.5 s in the narration track.
All edit points fall on word boundaries from the transcript.

title: Shot-boundary detection tuning
when: Finding cuts inside source clips (to avoid trimming across an internal cut) or measuring a reference video's shot lengths.
summary: Use a content-difference detector by default, an adaptive detector when the camera moves a lot, and a brightness-threshold detector only for fades through black. Tune from a per-frame statistics pass rather than guessing, enforce a minimum shot length and merge micro-shots.
steps: Run a statistics pass and inspect the per-frame difference values; peaks are cuts.
Set the threshold just below the smallest genuine peak.
Raise it for fast or animated content and lower it for static talking/presentation content.
Apply a minimum shot length; merge shorter segments into neighbours.
Map detected boundaries to narration pauses or script sections.
do: Use content detection for AI clips (they rarely fade through black).
Recalibrate thresholds when switching tools (e.g., FFmpeg scene scores use a 0-1 scale).
avoid: Using a threshold detector on footage without fades.
Trusting default thresholds on stylised animation.

numbers.animation: 30-35 (or weights hue 1.0, sat 0.5, luma 1.0, edges 0.2 at 32)
numbers.min_shot_length: 1.0 s default; 2-3 s educational; 0.5-1.0 s fast
numbers.presets: single-camera talk 22/3 s; multi-cam 27/1 s; screen 30/2 s; animated explainer adaptive 3.0/2 s; montage 40/0.5 s; doc with fades threshold 12/2 s

checks: No detected shot shorter than the minimum after merging.
Trim windows never straddle a detected internal cut.

title: Prompting AI images and clips with five aspects
when: Writing prompts for generated stills or video clips used as B-roll.
summary: Models describe subject and setting well but fumble motion, framing and camera, so always fill five slots: subject, subject motion, scene (overlays listed separately), spatial framing, and camera. Keep a shared visual system across shots via a hero reference image and a short adapted style anchor rather than pasting the same long prefix everywhere.
steps: Subject: type plus distinguishing attributes (repeat identity attributes verbatim across shots).
Subject motion: actions in time order.
Scene: point of view, setting, time of day, dynamics; overlays never described as foreground.
Spatial: shot size, position in frame, depth layers, camera height, and how they change.
Camera: speed (slow-mo, timelapse), lens, height, angle, focus, steadiness, movement.
Generate one hero image first and use it as reference for the rest; adapt the style anchor per scene.
Iterate: simple prompt first, then add camera, then lighting, then style; lock the seed once it works.
do: Keep dolly vs zoom and pan vs truck distinct; 'static' means no movement, focus change or zoom.
Describe what the camera reveals after a move.
For image-to-video, describe only motion, not appearance.
Name 3-5 anchor colours instead of 'warm tones'.
avoid: Readable text or logos in generated media.
Complex physics, crowds of talking characters, or 4+ simultaneous actions.
Conflicting lighting in one prompt.
Identical style prefix on every prompt (makes scenes samey).
Hands in detailed poses.
checks: Every generation prompt fills all five aspects or marks one N/A explicitly.
No prompt requests on-image text.
Prompt length within the model's band.

title: Channel taste dials and anti-default checks
when: Defining an editing style for a channel or a single video before planning shots.
summary: Write a specific design read (audience, promise, subject), then set three 1-10 dials: visual variance, motion intensity and information density. The dials drive layout variety, transition family, cut rhythm, hold length and callout density, and an anti-default list catches generic output.
steps: Write a design read tied to audience and promise (not just 'clean' or 'cinematic').
Set visual variance, motion intensity and information density (1-10).
Translate: high motion + low info -> short kinetic beats; low motion + high info -> stable frames, chart builds, long holds; high variance -> recurring anchors (type, palette, sound motif).
List anti-patterns to avoid for this channel.
Plan one reference still per scene family.
do: Keep a signature visual device scarce (one climactic beat, not every scene).
Ask: could this video belong to any topic after swapping the title? If yes, the style is too generic.
avoid: Generic purple AI gradients or default corporate blue with no subject reason.
The same transition on every cut when variance is 4+.
Busy, layered callouts on a channel whose information-density dial sits at 4 or below.
Kinetic motion that makes narration harder to follow.
One hero element reused as scaffolding in every scene.
checks: Design read is a sentence naming audience and promise.
Scene-to-scene primary subjects differ (no shared hero element across most scenes).
Transition variety and callout density respect the dials.

title: Tearing down a competitor/reference video
when: A reference or competitor video is supplied as 'make something like this'.
summary: Break the reference into measurable parts (content, style, structure, pacing) and a per-shot five-aspect breakdown, and classify whether its scenes are true motion clips, animated stills or static images, because that decides the production route. Keep what works, change at least one major element, and prove the direction with a short sample first.
steps: Sample keyframes (around 20) and detect shots; compute shot count and average shot length.
Classify each scene as motion clip, animated still (pan/zoom) or static image; never guess.
Describe each shot group by subject, motion, scene (overlays separately), framing and camera.
Extract what makes it work: hook technique, pacing, transitions, narration style, text style, palette.
Map needs to available capabilities and state gaps honestly.
Propose variants that keep some elements and change others (new subject, new angle, new visual treatment, new platform length, counter-take).
Produce a 10-15 s sample (hook + one middle scene) with real voice, visuals, music and caption style before full production.
do: Ground every claim about the reference in measured data.
Honour elements the user explicitly loved (e.g., pacing) and keep them measurable.
avoid: Carbon copies (same topic, structure and treatment).
Assuming the reference uses video generation when it uses animated stills (or vice versa).
Skipping the sample and discovering a style mismatch after full spend.

numbers.clip_strategy: prefer longer clips (e.g., 6 x 10 s for 60 s)

checks: Teardown lists motion type per scene and measured ASL.
Each proposed concept names what it keeps and what it changes.
Sample approved before batch production.
